paragraphs: Instruction tuning teaches a pretrained language model using examples of instructions and responses. This paper examines what that process actually changes, asking whether better conversational behavior also reflects improved knowledge or skills. Its experiments distinguish between LoRA tuning, which adjusts a restricted set of parameters, and tuning all model parameters.

In the studied settings, LoRA mainly learns how to begin responses and reproduce stylistic features. Full-parameter tuning instead degrades knowledge and increases hallucinations. The authors trace some incorrect responses to tokens borrowed from conceptually similar training examples. They also find that copying response patterns from knowledgeable sources can reduce response quality, despite the apparent quality of those sources.

The tested methods intended to improve instruction tuning do not outperform a simple LoRA model. Responses relying on pretrained knowledge consistently beat those incorporating new knowledge from the studied open-source instruction datasets. These findings separate learning a response format from learning reliable content, and identify ways instruction examples can interfere with knowledge already present in a model.
icml-2024-a-closer-look-at-the-limitatio.tldr: Experiments find that instruction tuning can teach response style while degrading factual knowledge and increasing hallucinations.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves an outer objective whose optimization depends on an inner problem. This paper studies a difficult stochastic setting: the outer objective is nonconvex and may have unbounded smoothness, while the inner objective is strongly convex. Sequential meta-learning motivates this setting because the outer loss's smoothness can grow with its gradient norm.

The proposed SLIP algorithm avoids repeatedly running nested optimization loops. After a few initial stochastic gradient steps on the inner variable, it updates both variables together. The outer update uses normalized stochastic gradients with momentum, while the inner update uses stochastic gradient descent. This design addresses the tuning burden associated with the existing nested approach.

Under the stated assumptions, SLIP reaches an epsilon-stationary point using roughly inverse-fourth-power dependence on epsilon in stochastic gradient or Hessian-vector calls, ignoring logarithmic factors. The result holds both in expectation and with high probability and is nearly optimal without requiring mean-square smoothness of the gradient oracle. The proof connects bilevel optimization to optimization under distributional drift, and experiments report substantial improvements over strong baselines.
icml-2024-a-nearly-optimal-single-loop-a.tldr: SLIP simplifies stochastic bilevel optimization to a single loop while retaining nearly optimal convergence guarantees under its assumptions.

paragraphs: Mixed linear regression fits a small collection of linear relationships to observations. Conventional analyses assume that each label was generated by randomly choosing one of several underlying linear functions, possibly adding noise. Success then means recovering those generating functions accurately. This paper asks what familiar algorithms can achieve when that account of the data is unavailable.

The authors study expectation maximization and alternating minimization in an agnostic setting, where the observations need not come from an assumed mixture-generating process. They show that these algorithms converge to population loss minimizers for suitably chosen losses. The guarantee still requires standard separation conditions and a good initialization.

This changes what the algorithms are justified as finding: a best fit according to the specified population objective, even when there are no true generating linear functions to recover. The result therefore extends their theoretical usefulness beyond correctly specified mixture models. Separation and initialization remain substantive conditions; removing the generative assumption does not make convergence unconditional.
icml-2024-agnostic-learning-of-mixed-lin.tldr: With separation and good initialization, EM and alternating minimization can learn mixed linear regressions without assuming a mixture-generating model.

paragraphs: Amortized Bayesian inference uses simulated examples to train a network that can answer inference questions quickly for new observations. Existing approaches often require many simulations and commit in advance to a particular prior, simulator, and inference task. This paper introduces Simformer to make that learned inference machinery more flexible.

Simformer combines a probabilistic diffusion model with a transformer architecture. It can sample different conditional distributions from the joint distribution of parameters and observations. This includes inferring parameters from data through a posterior, or generating data conditioned on parameters through a likelihood. The same framework also accommodates missing or unstructured observations and parameters that are functions.

The authors report better benchmark performance than current leading amortized inference approaches and demonstrate applications using ecological, epidemiological, and neuroscience simulators. The broader contribution is a method that supports multiple inference configurations within a common framework. Its ability to change what is observed and what is inferred expands the kinds of scientific questions that amortized simulation-based inference can address.
icml-2024-all-in-one-simulation-based-in.tldr: Simformer combines diffusion and transformers to support flexible simulation-based inference across parameters, observations, and missing-data settings.

paragraphs: Code has a grammatical structure that a simple sequence of tokens does not explicitly represent. AST-T5 uses abstract syntax trees to bring that structure into pretraining for code generation, translation between programming languages, and code understanding. Its central change concerns how training material and reconstruction tasks are prepared.

The method uses dynamic programming to segment code while retaining its structure. It then applies a structure-aware span corruption objective, training the model to reconstruct different code structures. These choices give the learning task information about how code is organized without requiring complex program analysis or changes to the model architecture. The approach can integrate with any encoder-decoder Transformer.

Evaluations report consistent improvements over similarly sized language models across code tasks, including HumanEval and MBPP. For code-to-code tasks, AST-T5 exceeds CodeT5 by two exact-match points on Bugs2Fix and three on Java-to-C# translation in CodeXGLUE. These results support the usefulness of incorporating syntax into pretraining, particularly when the output must preserve or transform an existing program's structure.
icml-2024-ast-t5-structure-aware-pretrai.tldr: AST-T5 improves code modeling by using syntax trees to structure pretraining examples and reconstruction tasks.

paragraphs: Most language models train to predict the next token at each position. This paper adds a broader prediction task: predict several upcoming tokens simultaneously. A shared model backbone feeds separate output heads, each responsible for one future token. The authors investigate whether this additional supervision helps models learn more effectively from their training data.

Across code and natural-language models, the experiments show improved downstream capabilities without additional training time. Benefits grow with model size and remain useful when training revisits the data over multiple epochs. Coding gains are particularly pronounced: the reported 13-billion-parameter models solve 12% more HumanEval problems and 17% more MBPP problems than comparable next-token models.

Small algorithmic experiments also indicate benefits for induction heads and algorithmic reasoning. Beyond training quality, four-token prediction enables inference speedups of up to threefold, including at large batch sizes. The findings make multi-token prediction relevant to both learning efficiency and generation speed, with the reported improvements tied to the evaluated model and task settings.
icml-2024-better-faster-large-language-m.tldr: Training models to predict several future tokens improves measured capabilities and enables inference speedups of up to threefold.

paragraphs: Radar-based precipitation nowcasting must follow weather systems that evolve at different spatial scales. Forecasting extreme rain adds another challenge: a model needs to capture localized patterns as well as the broader precipitation distribution. CasCast addresses these linked problems by dividing prediction into two connected stages.

The framework combines a deterministic component with a probabilistic component, separating mesoscale precipitation distributions from smaller-scale patterns. It explores high-resolution training while carrying out probabilistic modeling in a lower-dimensional latent representation. A diffusion transformer guided frame by frame supports this stage. The design aims to improve optimization for extreme events while reducing the computational cost of probabilistic prediction.

Experiments on three radar precipitation benchmarks show competitive overall performance. For regional extreme precipitation, the authors report improvements over the baseline reaching 91.8%. That figure is a reported maximum for this evaluation setting. The broader finding is that separating large-scale evolution from smaller probabilistic detail can help address the particular demands of high-resolution extreme-rain forecasting.
icml-2024-cascast-skillful-high-resoluti.tldr: CasCast separates broad precipitation evolution from small-scale probabilistic patterns to improve high-resolution nowcasting, especially for extreme rain.

paragraphs: Partial label learning trains classifiers with ambiguous candidate labels, some of which are incorrect. Deep models can become increasingly influenced by these false-positive labels as training proceeds. This paper examines whether label smoothing can reduce that problem and clarify how label ambiguity relates to classification performance.

The authors establish lower and upper bounds on expected risk to show that smoothing can help. They also derive an optimal smoothing rate and investigate the conditions under which the benefit occurs. This makes the amount of smoothing part of the theoretical question, rather than treating any smoothing setting as equally useful. They translate the analysis into a benchmark solution and an optimization algorithm called LS-PLL.

Experiments across partial-label datasets and different deep architectures report improvements in classification and in the distinctness of learned representations. The strongest results occur when the empirical smoothing rate approximately matches the theoretically optimal rate. Together, the theory and experiments support smoothing as a useful tool for ambiguous supervision, with its effectiveness depending on how strongly it is applied.
icml-2024-does-label-smoothing-help-deep.tldr: Theory and experiments show that appropriately chosen label smoothing can improve deep learning from ambiguous candidate labels.

paragraphs: Large diffusion models can generate paired images for training smaller GANs that perform image editing on mobile devices. However, each distilled GAN typically specializes in a particular editing concept, making support for many concepts expensive to train. E²GAN focuses on reducing that preparation cost while retaining efficient image editing.

The approach first trains a base GAN with features that can be adapted to different concepts. It then identifies important layers and applies Low-Rank Adaptation, using a rank search to choose the adaptation size. This avoids retraining a model from scratch or fine-tuning every parameter. The authors also investigate how little fine-tuning data is needed to reduce training time further.

Extensive experiments report real-time, high-quality mobile image editing with substantially lower training and storage costs per concept. The contribution therefore spans both model reuse and economical specialization. A reusable base model, selective parameter updates, and reduced data requirements work together to make producing a collection of specialized editing models less costly.
icml-2024-e-2-gan-efficient-training-of-.tldr: E²GAN reduces the cost of creating mobile image-editing GANs through a reusable base model, selective LoRA adaptation, and data-efficient fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Completing missing code inside a program requires using both the preceding and following context. SAFIM evaluates this ability through gaps aligned with program syntax, such as missing code blocks or conditional expressions. Its 17,720 examples span several programming languages and come from submissions after April 2022 to reduce potential training-data contamination.

The benchmark includes multiple prompt designs and syntax-aware post-processing methods intended to support accurate, fair comparisons. This matters because an evaluation of code completion needs to account for the program structure being completed, as well as how the model is prompted and how its output is processed.

The authors evaluate 15 language models and find that fill-in-the-middle pretraining improves both middle completion and left-to-right inference. Their results suggest that pretraining choices and data quality can matter more than model size. SAFIM consequently provides both an evaluation resource and evidence that the way code models are trained deserves close attention when interpreting differences in their completion abilities.
icml-2024-evaluation-of-llms-on-syntax-a.tldr: SAFIM evaluates syntax-aware code completion and finds evidence that pretraining methods and data quality can outweigh model size.

paragraphs: Protein representation models commonly learn by reconstructing a masked amino acid from a naturally occurring protein. That objective rewards identifying the existing residue, while protein engineering often aims to suggest a useful replacement. This paper addresses that mismatch by changing what the model is trained to predict.

Evolutionary Ranking, or EvoRank, uses evolutionary information from multiple sequence alignments. Its objective ranks amino-acid likelihoods according to the probability distribution induced by an alignment. Training therefore incorporates information about alternatives represented across related sequences, encouraging more diverse protein representations and learning about the protein's evolutionary dynamics.

Across several phenotypes and datasets, the authors report large improvements in zero-shot mutation-effect prediction. They also find that EvoRank can compete with models fine-tuned on experimental data. This matters because obtaining such data is expensive in protein engineering. The results support aligning the self-supervised objective more closely with mutation selection, while the comparison with fine-tuned models remains a reported empirical finding across the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-evolution-inspired-loss-functi.tldr: EvoRank trains protein models to rank evolution-informed amino-acid alternatives, improving zero-shot mutation-effect prediction.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization methods use noisy gradient information, and heavy-tailed noise makes strong reliability guarantees difficult. Gradient clipping is a common ingredient in high-probability analyses because it limits extreme updates. This paper identifies a complication: naive clipping can prevent convergence in composite or distributed optimization, even when there is no noise.

The authors propose methods that clip stochastic gradient differences. They analyze these methods for composite and distributed minimization and establish tight high-probability convergence results, including nearly optimal guarantees. The work addresses gaps in previous analyses, which often focused on unconstrained, nondistributed settings or omitted important cases such as strongly convex problems.

The paper also develops and analyzes corresponding methods for composite and distributed variational inequalities. Its contribution is both algorithmic and theoretical: the placement of clipping changes, and the resulting procedures receive guarantees suited to heavy-tailed noise. The central lesson is that controlling unusually large stochastic updates must be done in a way that preserves the optimization method's underlying convergence behavior.
icml-2024-high-probability-convergence-f.tldr: Clipping stochastic gradient differences enables tight high-probability guarantees for composite and distributed optimization with heavy-tailed noise.

paragraphs: Private optimization seeks useful solutions while limiting what an algorithm reveals about individual contributions to its input. This paper introduces a technique for tracking those privacy effects through subsampling. Its central observation is conditional: an algorithm satisfying one-sided add differential privacy has a subsampled variant satisfying two-sided differential privacy.

The authors use that conversion to improve algorithms for combinatorial optimization, including decomposable submodular maximization and set cover. Their algorithms achieve pure differential privacy, whereas the cited earlier approaches provided approximate differential privacy. They also establish asymptotically tight error guarantees, connecting the stronger privacy result with a precise account of solution accuracy.

The technique extends beyond those optimization problems to finding shifting heavy hitters in a data stream. Here too, the authors provide a pure-private algorithm where previously only an approximate-private one was known. Across these applications, the shared contribution is a reusable privacy-analysis step: prove the appropriate one-sided property, then use subsampling to obtain the two-sided guarantee.
icml-2024-individualized-privacy-account.tldr: A subsampling-based privacy conversion yields pure-private algorithms for several optimization and streaming problems.

paragraphs: Conditional biological sequence models generate sequences subject to supplied information. Evaluating them requires asking whether their output distribution matches the corresponding distribution in real data. This paper develops kernel-based tools for that task, with uses in model assessment, reliability evaluation, and hyperparameter selection.

The central quantity is Augmented Conditional Maximum Mean Discrepancy, or ACMMD. It measures a discrepancy between the true conditional distribution and the model's estimate. Provided samples can be drawn from the model, the quantity can be estimated without bias from data. It can then serve as a measure of absolute fit or be incorporated into a statistical hypothesis test.

The authors apply the tools to ProteinMPNN, a protein design model. For several protein families, their tests reject the hypothesis that the model fits its data. They also use the evaluation to adjust its temperature hyperparameter and improve fit. This demonstrates how a distribution-level assessment can both identify a mismatch and guide a concrete change to the model's sampling behavior.
icml-2024-kernel-based-evaluation-of-con.tldr: ACMMD measures conditional sequence-model fit and supports statistical testing and temperature tuning for protein design models.

paragraphs: Meta-learning trains a network across many tasks so that it can learn new ones from limited observations. This paper investigates how far that idea can be extended toward universal prediction. It takes Solomonoff Induction as its target and explores whether memory-based meta-learning can absorb broad prediction strategies into neural networks.

The authors generate training data using Universal Turing Machines, exposing networks to a wide range of algorithmically produced patterns. They theoretically analyze both the data-generation processes and the protocols used for meta-training. Experiments compare neural architectures, including LSTMs and Transformers, alongside generators that differ in complexity and universality.

The results suggest that Universal Turing Machine data is a useful resource for learning general prediction strategies. They also suggest that such data can train networks capable of learning universal prediction strategies. The contribution is an investigation of a route toward this goal through broad algorithmic experience; the stated findings do not establish that a trained network exactly implements Solomonoff Induction.
icml-2024-learning-universal-predictors-.tldr: The paper explores algorithmically generated meta-training data as a route toward neural networks that learn universal prediction strategies.

paragraphs: Continuous-time dynamic graphs represent relationships through events that arrive at irregular times. Some prediction tasks depend on information far from the current event, either across many graph connections or far back in time. The authors find that many existing message-passing, recurrent, and self-attention methods struggle with these long-range tasks.

They introduce the Continuous-Time Graph Anti-Symmetric Network, or CTAN, using an ordinary differential equation framework. Its design aims to propagate information efficiently so that distant events and higher-order node information can influence current predictions. The paper supplies theoretical findings supporting these long-range modeling capabilities.

Experiments on synthetic long-range tasks and real-world benchmarks report better performance than the compared methods. The results support CTAN's ability to carry relevant information across spatial and temporal distances in evolving graphs. They also motivate an evaluation change: temporal graph models should be tested explicitly on tasks requiring long-range dependencies, because those tasks expose weaknesses that are central to this modeling problem.
icml-2024-long-range-propagation-on-cont.tldr: CTAN uses a differential-equation framework to improve long-range information propagation in continuous-time dynamic graphs.

paragraphs: MOMENT is a family of open models intended for general-purpose time-series analysis. The paper addresses the infrastructure and learning challenges behind that goal: public datasets are fragmented, time series have diverse characteristics, and evaluation for settings with little supervision is still developing. These obstacles affect both pretraining and assessment.

The authors compile public datasets into a large, varied collection called the Time Series Pile. They also systematically address time-series-specific difficulties in training across datasets. Alongside the models and data collection, they develop a benchmark covering different tasks and datasets under limited supervision.

Experiments on that benchmark show that the pretrained models are effective with little data and limited task-specific fine-tuning. The contribution therefore combines reusable models with the data and evaluation framework needed to study them. This makes the paper relevant to whether shared pretraining can support varied time-series applications without requiring substantial labeled data or extensive adaptation for each individual task.
icml-2024-moment-a-family-of-open-time-s.tldr: MOMENT provides open time-series foundation models, a diverse pretraining collection, and evidence of effectiveness under limited supervision.

paragraphs: Untrained convolutional image generators can already favor useful image structure, making them effective priors for restoration. Their excess capacity, however, can also let them fit unwanted noise. Optimal Eye Surgeon addresses this by pruning a randomly initialized generator until it is underparameterized, before training its remaining weights.

The selected mask alone captures low-frequency image components, even without weight training. When the resulting subnetworks, called Sparse-DIP, are subsequently fitted to a noisy image, they resist overfitting to the noise. The authors attribute this behavior to reduced parameter capacity and the regularizing effect of masking, which constrains the network toward image priors.

Experiments show that OES-selected subnetworks outperform leading pruning approaches, including the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis approach, for image recovery. They also demonstrate mask transferability and investigate sparse subnetworks for image generation. The findings make the initial choice of retained connections an active part of restoration: sparsity shapes what the generator can represent before fitting begins and continues to constrain learning afterward.
icml-2024-optimal-eye-surgeon-finding-im.tldr: OES prunes image generators at initialization to retain useful image structure and reduce subsequent fitting of noise.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a dynamical system from time-series observations aims to recover rules governing its evolution. A model may capture long-term properties of the observed behavior yet fail in regions that were never observed. This paper asks how to define and assess that broader generalization, a capability expected of a useful scientific model.

The authors develop a formal framework using topology and ergodic theory to describe learnability in dynamical-system reconstruction. They explain why generalization beyond observed domains differs here from out-of-domain generalization elsewhere in machine learning. Within this framework, they prove that black-box deep learning generally cannot learn a generalizing reconstruction without adequate structural priors.

Empirical investigations of major reconstruction approaches illustrate failures to generalize across the whole phase space, the space of possible system states. These findings connect observed shortcomings to a mathematical account of the problem. The result places structural assumptions at the center of generalization, while leaving room for approaches that incorporate adequate priors to address the identified obstacles.
icml-2024-out-of-domain-generalization-i.tldr: A formal analysis shows why dynamical-system reconstruction generally needs adequate structural priors to generalize beyond observed states.

paragraphs: This position paper examines whether language-model defenses can reliably prevent responses with impermissible meaning. It focuses on fundamental verification problems behind fine-tuning and output censorship. The authors argue that failures of existing defenses motivate reconsidering what censorship should guarantee and how those guarantees should be defined.

They show that semantic censorship can be framed as an undecidable problem. They also identify conditions under which verifying an output's semantic properties can become impossible, including when a model can produce encrypted outputs. Another difficulty arises across multiple responses: individually permissible outputs can be combined to reconstruct an impermissible result.

These arguments challenge guarantees based only on judging the meaning of isolated responses. The paper calls for revised definitions and approaches, and offers an initial direction through syntactic censorship informed by security principles. Its position is that explicit restrictions on output form may support guarantees that semantic screening cannot generally provide, while the proposed direction is presented as an initial attempt.
icml-2024-position-fundamental-limitatio.tldr: The paper identifies fundamental obstacles to semantic output censorship and proposes exploring security-based syntactic guarantees.

paragraphs: No free lunch results say that no learner succeeds on every problem, or that learners have equal average accuracy under a uniform distribution over problems. These results are often used to argue for specialized biases tailored to each task. This position paper questions that interpretation when applied to real-world learning.

The authors emphasize that uniformly sampled datasets are usually highly complex, whereas real-world problems disproportionately produce simpler data. They use Kolmogorov complexity to formalize this distinction and argue that neural networks share a preference for low-complexity patterns. Experiments show that architectures designed for one domain can compress datasets from seemingly unrelated domains, and that both pretrained and randomly initialized language models favor low-complexity sequences.

The paper also explains how choices such as model size under different amounts of labeled data can be incorporated into a single learning algorithm. These observations support using a smaller collection of broadly applicable models across disparate tasks. The argument concerns shared structure in practical problems and does not claim to overturn the no free lunch theorems.
icml-2024-position-the-no-free-lunch-the.tldr: The paper argues that shared preferences for low-complexity data help explain broad neural-model usefulness despite no free lunch theorems.

paragraphs: When a generative model trains on machine-generated data, its outputs can feed back into later training. Such self-consuming loops may become unstable or collapse unless suitable conditions hold. This paper investigates whether correcting generated examples can make that feedback process more stable.

The theoretical analysis introduces an idealized correction function that moves a data point toward greater likelihood under the true data distribution. With this correction, the authors show that self-consuming loops can become exponentially more stable. They then propose practical approximations using expert knowledge, such as physical laws encoded in a simulator, to automate correction at scale.

Experiments on human motion synthesis show that the proposed self-correction avoids model collapse, including when the synthetic-to-real data ratio reaches 100%. This ratio describes equal amounts of synthetic and real data. The theoretical guarantee concerns the idealized corrector, while the motion experiments provide evidence for an expert-informed approximation. Together, they support correction as a way to improve the reliability of repeated training with generated examples.
icml-2024-self-correcting-self-consuming.tldr: Expert-informed correction stabilizes synthetic-data feedback loops in human motion experiments, supported by theory for an idealized corrector.

paragraphs: Image restoration often assumes that the kinds of degradation encountered during use were represented during training. Open-set restoration instead deals with previously unforeseen degradations. This paper interprets that challenge as an unidentified distribution shift between training images and the damaged image presented at test time.

The proposed framework has three components. A pretrained diffusion model supplies a degradation-agnostic model of clean images. A test-time adapter uses the input image to adapt to its unknown degradation. Finally, the adapter guides the diffusion model's restoration process toward a corresponding clean image. This connects a reusable clean-image model with adaptation to the particular input.

Across experiments involving multiple degradations, the method achieves performance comparable to, and sometimes better than, task-specific approaches. The results support adapting the degradation handling during inference when pretraining cannot anticipate the corruption encountered. The contribution is the integration of that adaptation with guided restoration, allowing the clean-image generator to be used in the studied open-set conditions.
icml-2024-test-time-degradation-adaptati.tldr: A test-time degradation adapter guides a pretrained diffusion model to restore images affected by previously unseen degradations.

paragraphs: A factually correct question-answer training set can still make a language model less factual. This paper studies how that outcome depends on whether the model stored the training facts well during pretraining. It finds that fine-tuning on poorly stored, lesser-known facts is worse than using well-known facts, even when pretraining included every fact.

The theoretical analysis explains a possible failure mechanism: learning from lesser-known facts can cause a model to disregard the subject entity's name and produce a generally plausible answer. This can happen even when the relevant knowledge is encoded in the model. Fine-tuning therefore affects how existing knowledge is accessed, as well as the responses the model learns to produce.

Experiments use PopQA, Entity Questions, and MMLU with Llama-2-7B and Mistral-7B. Fine-tuning on factual but lesser-known examples reduces downstream factuality by 5–10%, while better-known subsets match or outperform the full dataset. These results make the model's prior knowledge a relevant factor in selecting fine-tuning data; factual correctness of the examples alone does not ensure improvement.
icml-2024-understanding-finetuning-for-f.tldr: Fine-tuning on facts a model already knows well can preserve factuality better than training on correct but poorly stored facts.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor condensing replaces a larger labeled dataset with a smaller collection of representative points. New examples receive labels according to their nearest retained point. This paper extends that setup by assigning weights to the retained points and using weighted distances to decide which point supplies the label.

The authors analyze the resulting model and show that weighting can permit dramatically greater condensation than the standard nearest-neighbor rule. Despite that added flexibility, the model has generalization bounds almost identical to those of the unweighted approach. The result connects a potentially much smaller retained set with a similar theoretical account of prediction beyond the training data.

The paper then proposes a practical condensing heuristic for the weighted formulation. It establishes Bayes consistency for the heuristic, an asymptotic property concerning approach to the best possible classification error, and reports promising empirical results. The contribution combines a more flexible representation of the retained dataset with theoretical support and an algorithmic route to constructing it.
icml-2024-weighted-distance-nearest-neig.tldr: Weighted distances can substantially shrink nearest-neighbor representative sets while preserving similar generalization bounds.
